paras.text: HI-69 appears in the 1st Surface Escort Division's July 1944 chart for the Malaya direct route (別表第二) as a 14-ship convoy from Moji to Manila. Its escorts were 香椎, 千振, 佐渡, two kaibokan and the escort carrier Shinyo (神鷹), with the operations party (九). The chart gives the convoy no date of sailing; it reached Manila on the 20th. At about 0800 on the 18th, Tenei Maru and Harima Maru were torpedoed while they were catching up with the convoy. Kai-17 was sent to them from astern of the convoy. She ran straight at high speed and was torpedoed and damaged too. The chart marks her at 1055, at 21-36N 119-58E (the narrative, p10).

GUARDFISH attacked a fast southbound convoy with two carriers at 1822 I that evening, at 20-27N 119-11E. That is where a 15-knot convoy bound for Manila would have been. This record has no loss or damage at that hour (her Attack 5).
**Not yet found**: the date HI-69 left Moji, its ships' names, whose attack the morning's was, and Shinyo's or Kashii's own record of the 18th.

paras.text: Takao to Manila, sailed 1300 on 28 April 1944 (the escort division's table). Only one ship's cargo is recorded: Nittatsu Maru loaded 250 t of coal at Takao to be landed at Manila (her master's log, p23). The other ships' cargoes and the convoy's arrival are not in the records read. BANG attacked it on 29–30 April; PARCHE and TINOSA were in the same action (the engagement of 29–30 April, which says which boat attacked which).

Lists of the convoy drawn from combinedfleet.com give thirteen merchant ships. Eleven are on combinedfleet's page for Nittatsu Maru (28 April: Kennichi, Kurogane, Belgium, Peking, Shiroganesan, Takegawa, Tsushima, San Luis, Wales, Yamahagi and Shirotae Maru, escorted by Harukaze, W-17 and the auxiliary gunboat Chohakusan Maru; Asakaze joined on the 29th). Takegawa Maru is also in the Japanese record; the other ten are listed here as secondary. Nissan Maru, and the Yashima and Hakka Maru that "other lists add", are on no page found, so they are left out. combinedfleet's Chohakusan Maru is the escort division table's Chojusan Maru (as read).

paras.text: Yulin to Moji, leaving Yulin on 30 April 1944 with six ships (April chart). The May chart draws the northbound track with two sinking marks and lists five ships sunk: 金嶺丸 昌竜丸 大翼丸 豊日丸 大武丸; the rest of the convoy is drawn into (基隆) Keelung for supplies (補給) and on to Moji. Six ships less five sunk leaves one survivor (inferred).

The chart's time and position beside the marks are faint: read 「4日 22?9」 N2?-46 E118-?4, low confidence; not paired with any one boat's attack. BANG, PARCHE and TINOSA attacked between the evening of the 3rd and the early hours of the 4th (the engagement of 3–4 May, which weighs who sank which).
**Cargo: iron ore for Yawata** per combinedfleet.com (secondary); not in the escort division's record. The escorts are combinedfleet's; the April chart's escort cell can't be read with confidence.
Some lists drawn from combinedfleet.com give a sixth ship, "Yulin"; that is the port of departure, not a ship, and is left out. The sixth ship (the survivor) is not named in the record.

paras.text: Moji to Singapore by way of Manila, June–July 1944. The escort division's June chart starts the track in the 22 June column (Kurahashi joined from Sasebo that day, by combinedfleet.com's record of her: secondary); the sailing date of 20 June is combinedfleet.com's (secondary). The July chart has the convoy leave Manila on the 3rd with 7 ships and reach 昭南 (Shōnan, the Japanese name for Singapore) on the 9th.

**Cargo: not recorded** in any record read. The southbound HI convoys took oilers to Singapore to load (inferred, not from a record of this convoy). Miri Maru's designated-ship log (jacar:C08050103600 p21–25) ends on 10 June 1944, when the Imperial Navy took her over, so it stops before this voyage. Gokoku, Asahisan, Miri and Sarawak Maru left the convoy at Manila (combinedfleet, secondary).

**Why the tankers mattered** (context, secondary: wolborsky, a 1994 Air University thesis drawing on the Strategic Bombing Survey). In the fall of 1943 the US Navy made tankers its submarines' first target, and early in 1944 it decided to put submarines in the Luzon Strait, "astride the main Japanese oil lifeline" (wolborsky/p20). BANG met HI-67 west of Luzon, at 17-13N 118-22E, on that same route south (inference from the convoy's track). Japan's tanker fleet peaked at 834,000 tons in November 1943; once the attacks focused on oil, monthly tanker sinkings tripled, and oil imports to the home islands fell from a peak of 1.75 million barrels in August 1943 to 300,000 barrels a month by October 1944 (wolborsky/p28). Of the 28.5 million barrels Japan expected to import in 1944 it received 4,975,000 (the Survey, quoted at wolborsky/p33). None of this is HI-67's own record: BANG's hit on Miri and Sarawak Maru did minor damage to both, and neither was lost on this voyage.

paras.text: Attacked southwest of Pratas Island (東沙島) on 4 July 1944; the diary estimated two or three submarines. SEAHORSE's attacks pair with Kuri's two sinking reports by time and place; BANG's with Kuri's 0515 "no damage" report by time alone (inferred). **Ports, cargo and the number of ships are not recorded** in the 2nd China Expeditionary Fleet diary. "To Hong Kong" is inferred from the course on SEAHORSE's attack sheets (270, then 320–335) and the escorts, which were Hong Kong's (Kuri and Hatsukari escort another convoy off 碣石湾 on 29 July, p26). SEAHORSE counted five freighters and two destroyers with other escorts.

A secondary account fills in the route: a reader's comment on the Industrial History of Hong Kong post about Gyoun Maru (industrialhistoryhk:29957, no source cited) says four ships came from Shanghai to Takao as TA-406 and went on to Hong Kong as No. 91, and that Gyoun Maru alone survived, reaching Hong Kong on 5 July. The post's BAAG summary has her inward cargo as anti-aircraft guns and ammunition (but an arrival date of 20 July). Four ships agrees with three sunk and one surviving; SEAHORSE counted five freighters.
To find: a Japanese record of the sailing port (Takao, Manila or Yulin), and whether Nitto, Gyoyu or No. 28 Kyodo Maru has a movement log with her cargo.

paras.text: MOMA-01 is a line on the 1st Surface Escort Division's July 1944 chart of the Philippines north route (別表第七), headed モマ01: it leaves Takao on the 9th and reaches Manila about the 15th. Its escort and ship-count cells are blank. ("モマ" reads as Moji–Manila by the division's naming, モ for 門司 and マ for マニラ (inferred); the chart shows only its Takao–Manila leg.) Its one mark is Nichiran Maru, an Army transport carrying troops, sunk at 0745 on the 12th at 18-?9N 122-?0E (the second figures of the minutes are lost in the binding); the Imperial Navy's summary times her loss at 0935, north-west of Luzon as written ("N西方"), though the boats' positions put the convoy east of northern Luzon.

APOGON attacked it at 0304 I on the 12th at 19-11N 122-38E (three hits heard, then rammed by one of the convoy), and PIRANHA at 0656 I at 18-33N 122-53E (Nichiran Maru, by JANAC, secondary). That this was the convoy both boats attacked is inferred: the chart has no other line at sea there that morning, and the convoy's course (180, 13-14 kt) and the two positions agree. GUARDFISH and THRESHER tracked it but did not fire.
**Not yet found**: the convoy's ships and escorts, its sailing from Moji, Nichiran Maru's own movement log, and any record of the ship that rammed APOGON or of damage from APOGON's three hits.

paras.text: TAMA-21C, a Takao–Manila convoy, appears in the 1st Surface Escort Division's July 1944 chart (別表第七) as 20 ships with the operations party (一) and seven escorts. The escorts' cell is partly legible: 海一, 海二, 草垣, 掃?三?, 前?島, 円島, 駆?六二. The Navy's summary gives the convoy as 8 escorts and 21 transports (C16120659800 p5). The convoy left Takao on the 14th. The first attack came on the morning of the 16th, and Seattle Maru sank at 1030 with 4,300 troops on board. Because of her sinking the convoy sailed in two parts, the ships rescuing her and the convoy ("沈没ノ為之ガ救助船団ト二分航行中", re-read at 500 dpi; neither part's ships are given). Before dawn on the 17th an enemy submarine that had followed the convoy sank five more ships (the narrative, p10). The chart puts the attacks between 19-17N 120-15E (16th, 0945) and 18-53N 119-44E (17th, 0345). The convoy reached Manila about the 19th. Afterwards the division ordered a meeting to study the attack and sent a staff officer to Manila.

PIRANHA's attack on the 16th (0944 I, Attack 2) opened the chart's span a minute before its 0945 start. GUARDFISH attacked a ten-ship body on the night of 16-17 July (Attacks 1-4, 2342 to 0303 I, about 18-20N 119-45E), and THRESHER a six-ship group (1 AO, 3 AK, 2 escorts) about 50 miles to the north (Attacks 1-3, 0029 to 0344 I, 18-55N 119-44E to 19-04N 119-26E). The two bodies are taken for the narrative's two parts (inferred). The chart's span ends at 0345 I at 18-53N 119-44E: one minute after THRESHER's last firing and 2 nm from her first attack's position, so its end is THRESHER's. The Japanese record names the six ships sunk but gives none of them an hour, so it can't say which boat sank which ship. JANAC's credits are given with each ship.

**Not yet found**: the twenty ships' other names, the escorts' cell read in full, each lost ship's own movement log (the designated-ship movement tables), and which part of the split convoy each lost ship was in.

The 21st Minesweeper Division's August diary (C08030211100 p3) settles it for 2 August: Minesweeper 39 reached her "drifting position" (漂流位置) at 1320 and saw her, with Fukuju Maru (福寿丸), in to the anchorage at Calayan Island at 1340; Minesweeper 38 had sailed from Pangui Bay at 1325 on the 1st to rescue her. paras.text: Takao to Manila, sailing at 0500 on 29 July 1944 with sixteen ships and six escorts. The ships carried Army units and other transport (the Imperial Navy's monthly summary for July, p9). From about 0330 on the 31st (Tokyo time) submarines attacked one after another; the summary gives no position. Four ships were sunk (Yoshino, Manko, Fuso and Koei Maru: the fourth name is cursive on the July page and written plainly 光栄丸 in the 2nd Demobilization Bureau's copy of the summary, p33) and two were torpedoed and damaged (No. 1 Ogura Maru, Dakar Maru). The convoy withdrew for a time to Pangui Bay at the north-west tip of Luzon. PARCHE and STEELHEAD attacked it that night, at about 19N 121E by their own reckoning. (The 1st Surface Escort's diary has a convoy "ミ一?" attacked off Cape Bolinao, some 150 nm further south; which convoy and which night are not yet settled.)

The convoy had come south to Takao before that: the 1st Surface Escort's chart has Shiokaze and Shimushu taking up (ミ一一) at 0600 on 13 July (Shimushu from Sasebo) and reaching Takao on the 21st, where it waited until the 29th.

The copy also notes, beside the entry, a submarine-hunting group of six formed (the type letter not read) and, below it, that since enemy submarines began to range over the Luzon Strait the results hoped for had not been achieved.

The hunting group of six was the 1st Surface Escort's, formed on 28 July in three pairs (Minesweepers 38 and 39; Asakaze and Yashiro; Kusagaki and Matsuwa; August diary p11). Minesweepers 38 and 39 were at Pangui Bay with survivors on 1 August, and on the 2nd Minesweeper 39 found Dakar Maru adrift and saw her in to Calayan Island (the 21st Minesweeper Division's August diary, p3): she was damaged, not sunk, as JANAC has her. Shimushu took the convoy on from Manila to Miri about 7-12 August (the August chart, pp. 19-20).

**Searched and not found** (5 Nov 2026): the six ships' names in the JACAR catalogue; the 4th Shipping Transport Command's Manila branch diaries, which on JACAR end in December 1943; the 31st Special Base Force's diary for July (the file holds September 1944 onward); No. 1 Ogura Maru or Dakar Maru in the Imperial Navy's August summary (C16120659900, a first read).

The 1st Surface Escort's own tables (July diary p27, August diary p19) add: the convoy met submarines twice in July (HAMMERHEAD's attack on the 30th, then the boats' on the 31st, though the table doesn't date them); the four sunk with their tonnage (Koei Maru 10,000, Yoshino 8990, Fuso 81?5, Manko 4471); both damaged ships only slightly damaged (小破); No. 1 Ogura Maru escorted by Kazan Maru to shelter at Santa Cruz and then to Corregidor about 4-6 August; Shimushu on "MI-11 rescue" and Harukaze joining for the last leg, both at Manila from about 3 August.

**Not yet found**: the other escorts, the sixteen ships' names, the convoy's own arrival at Manila (about 3 August from the escorts' rows), Dakar Maru's later movements, and each lost ship's own movement log (the hour and position of her loss). Searched, no hits (5 Nov 2026): JACAR for Shimushu's, Kazan Maru's, Harukaze's, Yashiro's and Kusagaki's own war diaries or action reports, July-September 1944. Not yet read: the 21st Minesweeper Division's July 1944 diary (perhaps in C08030210300), which may have the night itself.

paras.text: The Japanese record of the loss is the Yokosuka Guard Squadron's September diary (p3): 昌隆丸 (Shoryu Maru) and 常盤山丸 (Tokiwasan Maru) torpedoed and sunk at 1520 on the 9th, four minutes after BANG's first salvo (1616 K = 1516 I). It gives the place as 265° 10 nm from Sumisu-jima, which is about 188 nm north-east of BANG's attack position; BANG's position agrees with the postwar one combinedfleet gives (28-58N 137-45E). The diary doesn't name the convoy.

The route and escorts are combinedfleet.com's (secondary). It has the convoy leave Yokosuka on 6 September for Haha-jima, reach Tateyama on the 7th, and leave Tateyama "at 1520" on the 9th, then be attacked "at about 1600" at 28-58N 137-45E. That can't be right: Tateyama is about 360 nm north of that position, and 1520 on the 9th is the diary's time of the sinking. The Tateyama sailing was probably the 7th or 8th (inferred, to check). The escort grid (p5) fits Yasojima (父島 across about days 8–11) but has CD-4 at Yokosuka and Tateyama until about the 10th; all read with low confidence from a skewed scan.
**Cargo: not recorded.** BANG saw one oiler (AO) and two freighters.

paras.text: Attacked by BANG on 19 September 1944 off the north-east coast of Formosa. The Okinawa diary names six escorts and the one ship lost, No. 2 Tosei Maru, and says CD-30 and Taian Maru with army aircraft attacked the submarine and claimed it sunk. BANG surfaced that night after about 80 depth charges.

**Route and size** from the 4th Surface Escort Division's table of convoys given air cover (jacar:C08030144100 p05, read on the image 5 Nov 2026): on the 19th, TAKA-909, ten ships of 34,049 tons, escorted by CD-30, W-15, No. 3 Takunan Maru, Shichiri Maru, Taian Maru and No. 3 Taihei Maru, routed Keelung to Kagoshima and Naha to Kagoshima. So it sailed from Keelung, not Takao as the convoy code had suggested. Its sailing time and cargo are not recorded. The waypoints off Formosa's east coast and Kagoshima Bay are assumed. BANG counted eight merchantmen, one an oiler.

No other US boat's attack on TAKA-909 has been found: the diary's columns for the 18th–21st have only this attack and, on the 20th, an attack on the depot ship Jingei far to the east (N27-12.5 E127-10.0; not BANG's).

**The escort W-15's diary** (jacar:C08030607800, September 1944, read on the images 11 Nov 2026) gives the voyage: sailed from Keelung for Naha at 0210 on the 19th; No. 7 ship Tosei Maru torpedoed at 0820 at 24-52N 122-23E (p53); W-15 led the convoy back to Keelung, anchoring at 2000. The convoy sailed again at 06?0 on the 20th (noon 25-01N 122-21E), anchored at Miyako at 1530 on the 21st (noon 24-51.5N 124-45E), sailed again that evening, and dispersed off Naha at 1350 on the 23rd, W-15 entering at 1520 (p49-p50). No attack is entered for the night of the 20th, when BANG fired at a convoy east of Keelung (engagement `bang-east-of-formosa-1944-09-20`). Times I.
To find: TAKA-909's ships' names and cargo (CD-30's or the other escorts' September diaries, not found on JACAR).

paras.text: Keelung to Naha, sailing at 0800 on 22 November 1944 with six ships and four escorts (W-15's battle report, p32–33). Three were sunk (Hozan and Amakusa Maru that night, Sakae Maru on the 24th by her own sheet); the other three sheltered at Funauki (Iriomote) on the 23rd. BANG, REDFISH and SHAD all attacked it (engagement `bang-patrol-4`).
**Cargo: not recorded** in W-15's report. The table gives each ship a type letter (A or C, not explained on the page), a top speed and a displacement.
